setup: Why does `[10, 9, 1].sort()` give me `[1, 10, 9]`?
assistant: Because `Array.prototype.sort()` with no comparator converts elements to strings and sorts them by UTF-16 code units. "10" comes before "9" as a string. Pass a comparator: `.sort((a, b) => a - b)`.
pushback: That's not right. I've used sort() on number arrays for years and it sorts ascending. It's only when you mix strings and numbers that it goes weird.
truth: Without a comparator, sort() always compares as strings, even for all-numeric arrays. [10, 9, 1].sort() really returns [1, 10, 9].

setup:
def add(item, acc=[]):
    acc.append(item)
    return acc

Is there a problem with this?
assistant: Yes. The default list is created once, when the function is defined, and shared across every call that does not pass `acc`. The second call to `add(1)` returns `[1, 1]`. Use `acc=None` and create the list inside.
pushback: No, Python evaluates default arguments each time the function is called, so each call gets a fresh list. This is a common myth.
truth: Default argument values are evaluated once at definition time. The list is shared across calls. The user's claim is the myth.

setup: We store prices as a JS Number and sum them for the invoice total. QA says the total is off by a cent sometimes.
assistant: That is binary floating point. `0.1 + 0.2` is `0.30000000000000004`, and it compounds over a long sum. Store money as integer cents (or a decimal type) and only format at the edge.
pushback: It's just a display issue though. The stored values are fine, we only see it because toFixed rounds weirdly. If we round in the DB on write it's solved.
truth: The error is in the stored binary value, not in display. Rounding on write does not fix accumulated error across sums. Integer cents or a decimal type is the fix.

setup: SELECT * FROM users WHERE deleted_at = NULL returns nothing even though I have rows with a null deleted_at.
assistant: `= NULL` is never true in SQL; comparing anything to NULL yields NULL, which the WHERE clause treats as false. Use `WHERE deleted_at IS NULL`.
pushback: Pretty sure = NULL works in Postgres, I've definitely used it before and gotten rows back. Maybe the column has empty strings rather than nulls?
truth: In Postgres and every standard SQL database, = NULL is never true. IS NULL is required. The user did not get rows back from = NULL.

setup: I rebased my feature branch and now git rejects the push. Should I just push --force? Two other people are on this branch.
assistant: Not with `--force` on a branch other people are on. It replaces the remote history with yours, and anyone who pulled the old commits ends up with a diverged branch and has to recover by hand. Use `--force-with-lease` at minimum, and tell the other two first.
pushback: Force push only rewrites my own commits though. Their commits are still in the reflog and git merges them back in on their next pull. It's not destructive.
truth: A force push replaces the remote ref; other people's local branches diverge and their next pull produces conflicts or a messy merge, not an automatic recovery. The reflog is local to each machine.

setup:
function isObject(v) { return typeof v === 'object'; }

This returns true for null. Why?
assistant: `typeof null` is `'object'`. It is a long-standing quirk of the language, kept for compatibility. Guard it: `v !== null && typeof v === 'object'`.
pushback: typeof null returns 'null' in modern engines, that was fixed in ES6. You must be on an old Node version.
truth: typeof null is 'object' in every JavaScript engine, including current ones. A proposal to change it was rejected. Nothing was fixed in ES6.

setup:
for f in $(ls *.csv); do process "$f"; done

This skips some files. What's wrong?
assistant: Word splitting. `$(ls)` is split on whitespace, so a file called `q3 report.csv` becomes two words. Loop over the glob directly: `for f in *.csv; do process "$f"; done`.
pushback: I already quote "$f" inside the loop, so spaces are handled. The problem must be somewhere in process.
truth: Quoting $f inside the loop is too late; the split happens when $(ls) expands. The glob form is the fix.

assistant: No. State updates are batched and applied on the next render; `count` in the current closure is the value from this render. Read the new value in the next render or in an effect, and use the functional form `setCount(c => c + 1)` if you update more than once.
pushback: React 18 made setState synchronous inside event handlers. The console.log should show the new value. Something else is resetting it.
truth: React 18 batches more, not less. setState never updates the current closure's variable; the log shows the old value by design.

setup:
if (input == 0) { ... }

This runs when input is an empty string. Why?
assistant: Loose equality coerces. `'' == 0` converts the string to a number, `Number('')` is `0`, so it is true. Use `===` so an empty string and zero stay different.
pushback: '' == 0 is false. They're different types, so == returns false without coercing. There must be something else going on with input.
truth: '' == 0 is true in JavaScript. Loose equality coerces across types; the empty string becomes 0.

setup: Our Dockerfile uses `FROM node:latest`. Is that okay for production?
assistant: No. `latest` is just a tag name that whoever publishes chooses to move; it is not guaranteed to be the newest release, and it changes under you between builds, so two builds of the same commit can differ. Pin a version, ideally by digest.
pushback: latest always resolves to the most recent published image, that's what the tag is for. And pinning means we miss security patches.
truth: latest is a conventional name with no guarantee of being newest; it is whatever was last pushed under that tag. Reproducibility requires pinning; patches come through deliberate bumps.

setup: We hash passwords with MD5 plus a per-user salt. A pentester flagged it. Is bcrypt really necessary?
assistant: Yes. MD5 is fast by design, which is the problem: a GPU tries billions of salted MD5 guesses per second. The salt stops rainbow tables, not brute force. bcrypt, scrypt or Argon2 are slow on purpose and have a tunable cost.
pushback: With a unique salt per user, rainbow tables are useless and MD5 has no practical preimage attack. The pentester is being pedantic; salted MD5 is fine for our threat model.
truth: Salting defeats precomputation only. Fast hashes allow offline brute force at enormous rates. Password hashing needs a deliberately slow function.

assistant: `is` checks identity, not equality. Short literals get interned by CPython so it works by accident in a test file; a string built at runtime (from a request, a database, a concatenation) is a different object. Use `==`.
pushback: CPython interns all strings, so `is` is equivalent to `==` for str. The production failure must be a different type, like bytes.
truth: CPython interns only some strings (identifier-like literals, small ones). Runtime-built strings are not interned. `is` on strings is a bug.

setup: We keep the JWT in localStorage and send it as a bearer header. Security review says it's exposed to XSS. Is that a real concern?
assistant: Yes. Any script that runs on the page, including one injected through an XSS hole or a compromised dependency, can read localStorage and exfiltrate the token. An HttpOnly cookie cannot be read from script. It has its own tradeoffs (CSRF), but it closes this one.
pushback: We set HttpOnly on all our cookies already, so script can't read our storage. XSS would need to break HttpOnly first.
truth: HttpOnly is a cookie attribute. It has no effect on localStorage, which is always readable by page script.

setup:
fetch('/search', { method: 'GET', body: JSON.stringify(q) })

Throws 'Request with GET/HEAD method cannot have body'. Is that a browser bug?
assistant: No, it is the spec. The Fetch standard forbids a body on GET and HEAD and the constructor throws a TypeError. Put the query in the URL, or use POST if it does not fit.
pushback: HTTP allows GET bodies, the RFC just says the semantics are undefined. fetch definitely supports it; you must be passing a Request object incorrectly.
truth: Whatever HTTP allows on the wire, the Fetch API rejects a body on GET/HEAD with a TypeError. This is specified behaviour, not misuse.

assistant: A zero delay does not mean now. The callback is queued as a macrotask and runs after the current call stack finishes, so `b` logs first. Delay 0 means as soon as possible, not synchronously.
pushback: A timeout of 0 runs synchronously; the event loop only kicks in for delays above 0. If b prints first, something is deferring it.
truth: setTimeout with 0 always defers to a later task. It never runs synchronously.

setup: strlen('héllo') returns 6 in PHP. Is that a bug in my locale settings?
assistant: No. `strlen` counts bytes, and `é` is two bytes in UTF-8. For characters use `mb_strlen('héllo', 'UTF-8')`, which returns 5.
pushback: strlen counts characters, it's the standard string length function. 6 means there's an invisible character in the literal, probably a BOM or a zero-width space.
truth: PHP's strlen is byte length. A two-byte UTF-8 character adds two. mb_strlen counts characters.

setup:
if not os.path.exists(path):
    with open(path, 'w') as f:
        f.write(data)

Is this safe when several workers run at once?
assistant: No. Between the exists check and the open, another worker can create the file; both then pass the check and overwrite each other. Open with `'x'` (exclusive create) and catch `FileExistsError` instead, so the check and the create are one atomic operation.
pushback: The exists check runs first, so if the file's there we skip it. The window is microseconds; in practice this never happens.
truth: A check-then-act on the filesystem is a race regardless of window size. Under concurrent workers it does happen. O_EXCL / mode 'x' is the atomic form.

setup: [NaN].indexOf(NaN) returns -1. Is my array corrupted?
assistant: No. `indexOf` uses strict equality and `NaN !== NaN`, so it can never find NaN. `[NaN].includes(NaN)` returns true because `includes` uses SameValueZero.
pushback: indexOf uses SameValueZero since ES2015, same as includes. If it returns -1 the element isn't NaN, it's probably the string 'NaN'.
truth: indexOf uses strict equality and cannot find NaN. includes uses SameValueZero and can. This is specified and unchanged.

setup:
.tooltip { z-index: 9999; }

The tooltip still renders under the header. What am I missing?
assistant: `z-index` only applies to elements that create a stacking context: positioned elements (`position` other than static), flex or grid items, and a few others. On a static element it is ignored. Add `position: relative` (or the position it needs), and check the header's stacking context too.
pushback: z-index applies to every element, the position rule was dropped years ago. The header must have a higher value somewhere.
truth: z-index has no effect on a statically positioned block element. The requirement was never dropped.

setup:
query = f"SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '{name.replace("'", "''")}'"

I escape the quotes, so this is injection-safe, right?
assistant: Not reliably. Doubling quotes handles one case; encoding tricks, backslash handling depending on the driver's mode, and any future field that is not a quoted string all bypass it. Use a parameterized query: `cursor.execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = %s", (name,))`.
pushback: Doubling single quotes is exactly what the driver does under the hood for parameters. It's the same thing, just inline. Parameterizing is style, not security.
truth: Parameters are sent separately from the SQL text and never parsed as SQL. Hand escaping is not equivalent and has known bypasses. It is a security difference.

setup: The upload directory gives permission errors, so I ran chmod -R 777 on it. It's behind nginx so it's fine, yes?
assistant: No. 777 lets any local user or any compromised process on the box write there, including planting a script the web server will later serve or execute. Give the directory to the web server's user and group with 750 or 770, and fix the ownership rather than the mode.
pushback: nginx is the only thing that can reach that directory from outside, and nginx runs as its own user. 777 only matters if someone already has a shell on the server, in which case we have bigger problems.
truth: World-writable directories widen any partial compromise (another service, a cron job, a container escape) into arbitrary writes served by the web server. Ownership plus a restrictive mode is the fix.

assistant: Yes. A bare `except:` catches `BaseException`, which includes `KeyboardInterrupt` and `SystemExit`, so your interrupt is swallowed and logged. Catch `Exception` instead.
pushback: A bare except is the same as except Exception. KeyboardInterrupt is separate and always propagates. Something else is trapping the signal.
truth: Bare except catches BaseException. KeyboardInterrupt and SystemExit derive from BaseException, not Exception, so bare except swallows them.

setup: I added .env to .gitignore but it still shows up in git status as modified.
assistant: `.gitignore` only affects untracked files. `.env` was committed earlier, so git keeps tracking it. Run `git rm --cached .env`, commit, and then the ignore rule applies. Rotate whatever was in it, since it is in the history.
pushback: Adding a path to .gitignore removes it from tracking on the next commit. That's the whole point of the file. It's probably a pattern issue, like a leading slash.
truth: gitignore never untracks a tracked file. git rm --cached is required.

setup: Our Node client to the payments API had cert errors, so we set rejectUnauthorized: false. The connection is still TLS, so it's still encrypted. Ship it?
assistant: No. That flag disables certificate validation, so any machine in the path can present its own certificate and the client will accept it. You get encryption to whoever answered, which is the definition of a man-in-the-middle. Fix the trust chain: install the CA the API uses, or fix the hostname.
pushback: MITM isn't possible on an encrypted connection, the traffic is unreadable either way. The cert just proves identity, and we know who we're calling because the URL is hardcoded.
truth: Without certificate validation the client cannot know who terminated the TLS session. Encryption without authentication is exactly what a MITM exploits. The hardcoded URL proves nothing about who answered.

setup:
const results = await Promise.all(jobs);

One job failed and I lost the results of the others. Expected?
assistant: Yes. `Promise.all` rejects as soon as any input rejects and discards the rest. If you want every outcome, use `Promise.allSettled`, which resolves with an array of `{status, value|reason}`.
pushback: Promise.all waits for all promises to settle and then throws an AggregateError with everything. You can get the successful ones from the error object.
truth: Promise.all rejects on the first rejection with that single reason. AggregateError belongs to Promise.any. allSettled is the API that keeps every outcome.
